title: bursting-reuse-anomaly-replay-and-ssd-tier-probe
body:
Objective:
This note captures the replay-driven investigation into intermittent reuse-rate collapses observed in production during short bursts. The aim: reproduce a deterministic workload that triggers the anomaly, measure how eviction/paging behavior interacts with limited NVMe/SSD spillback thresholds, and quantify memory-bandwidth-induced amplification of cold misses.

Context / Motivation:
Over the last two quarters we've seen a small-but-stable class of SLO-impacting incidents where tail latency and token-cost jump for a subset of requests during traffic bursts. Telemetry points to a sudden drop in KV cache reuse for ~30–120s windows. Existing telemetry is noisy: sampling, rate-limits in metrics pipeline, and mixed multi-tenant interference make root cause hypotheses weak. Rather than keep iterating on live blames, we built a deterministic replayer that can inject production traces with controlled burst parameters and a tunable SSD spillback threshold in the lab.

High-level hypothesis:
1) Short bursts (spike factor >= 4x baseline for 5–45s) create eviction waves that evict recently-warm entries due to bandwidth-driven prioritization.
2) When SSD/SSD-QoS/driver throttle engages (simulated 'ssd-tier threshold'), backpressure increases host-side read amplification and interleaves with DMA latency, causing reuse rates to collapse.
3) Mixed-seqLen workloads exacerbate thrashing because long-seq requests push hot KV pages into the eviction horizon and block small request hot keys.

Replayer approach (deterministic):
- Source trace: anonymized request trace from 2024-09-12 incident (extracted hotkey hashes, seqLen distribution, per-request token counts).
- Deterministic time dilation: replayer speeds/squashes inter-arrival times to produce spikes with reproducible relative ordering.
- Multi-tenant mixing: synthetic background streams (low-cost freq=0.5–2 rps) to simulate noisy co-tenants.
- SSD model: a parametric latency/bandwidth model that can simulate QD-dependent latency cliffs and a configurable throttling threshold (IOPS and MB/s).
- Kernel instrumentation: perf counters + nvme-cli synthetic workload hooks + custom driver-level latency hooks (lab kernel).

Experiment matrix:
Axis A (burst): none | 2x | 4x | 8x peak
Axis B (burst duration): 5s | 20s | 60s
Axis C (ssd-tier threshold): unconstrained | 80% bw cap | 50% bw cap | 30% bw cap
Axis D (mixed seqLen): single-homogeneous | 70/30 short/long | heavy-long (40% > 1024 tokens)
Each cell run 6x (to catch non-deterministic noise).

Key metrics collected:
- per-request reuse-rate (prefix kv hits / total kv lookups) sampled at 1s
- eviction-rate (pages evicted/sec), page-size granularity
- avg & p95 token completion latency
- nvme read latency distribution and QD breakdown
- memory bandwidth per GPU host-channel (via pcm and gpu-bw counters)
- kernel stalls and syscall latency (samples/sec)
- spillback read-amplification (read MB per logical KV miss)
- CPU load and IRQ time during bursts

Preliminary results (summary):
- Reuse collapse correlates strongly with SSD bandwidth saturation thresholds. When ssd-tier is restricted to 50% nominal bandwidth, reuse-rate drops by 45–70% during spikes, compared to <10% impact when unconstrained.
- Eviction waveform: eviction-rate ramps up with ~200–400ms lag after burst start. This matches the observed production timing.
- Read amplification: under congested SSD model, single logical miss triggers ~1.6–2.2x MB reads due to sub-page IO or non-coalesced reads; combined with DMA queue latency this reduces effective throughput and keeps pages from warm re-insertion.
- Memory bandwidth contention: when mixed long-seq requests are present, GPU host memory channels saturate intermittently, increasing page-fault servicing time (observed via higher syscalls for page reclaim) and amplifying eviction oscillations.

Notable traces (examples):
- Run B4 (8x burst, 20s, ssd 50%, mixed-heavy): immediate 60% reuse drop at 7s, eviction-rate peak at 9s (~3.2k pages/s), NVMe 95th latency climbs from 6ms to 120ms. System enters degraded reuse state for 83s post-burst as rewarm is slow.
- Run C2 (4x burst, 5s, ssd unconstrained, single-homogeneous): minor reuse drop (8%), eviction-rate spikes briefly, rewarm in <10s.

Interpretation / mechanistic model:
- Two-layer bottleneck: (1) fast eviction wave triggered by burst-induced working set expansion; (2) slow spillback path (NVMe throttle) that increases miss service time and effectively prevents pages from being re-inserted before other requests displace them.
- The bandwidth model indicates a critical threshold where miss-service-time exceeds median inter-arrival for warm keys; beyond that point reuse collapses nonlinearly.

Open questions and uncertainties:
- Are there driver-level coalescing opportunities that would reduce read amplification? Our NVMe model is conservative; real driver behavior across instance types may vary. Need partner infra to test on GCP/AWS with real NVMe tails.
- Does CPU IRQ affinity and NAPI scheduling play a role? Some runs showed large IRQ-time increases; need to try pinning IRQs to dedicated cores.
- Multi-tenant fairness: can a tenant burst be throttled at admission rather than relying on spillback to protect global reuse?

Action items / next experiments:
1) Implement read-coalescing patch in replayer (group adjacent key reads into single IO when contiguous) and re-run critical cells. Owner: Liang — ETA 2025-02-14.
2) Reproduce on cloud hardware (m.2 NVMe vs ephemeral local SSD) to validate driver differences. Engage infra: Tomoko to open infra ticket.
3) Try IRQ/core pinning test matrix to see if IRQ latency explains longer-than-modeled miss service. Owner: Marta — ETA 2025-02-21.
4) Evaluate an admission-side mitigation: short token-return fallback where short requests hit a small in-memory bloom cache to reduce miss thundering. Prototype in kv-replayer PR 78. Owner: Evan.
5) Telemetry: ship a lightweight high-sample (1s) reuse-rate metric for affected routes for 2 weeks to better correlate field incidents. Owner: SRE / Observability.

Immediate mitigations considered (pros/cons):
- Increase SSD headroom: reduces cost and requires infra changes (low friction short-term for Dedicated clusters).
- Conservative eviction hysteresis: keep a fraction of recently-evicted pages pinned for X seconds post-burst — reduces cache churn but increases memory footprint (needs cost analysis).
- Admission shaping during bursts: throttling large-seq requests when KV reuse drops — complex policy and risk of degrading some customer experience.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working artifact — many traces/plots attached in the replayer artifacts (see GH PR and Confluence). The runbook for replayer is in CONFLUENCE: SERVING-RUNTIME/kv-replay-harness.
- If you reproduce locally please use the same pinned kernel image (sha256: 8f9a...) and nvme firmware shim referenced in GH PR.

Appendix (quick checklist for reproducing run B4):
- checkout GH PR branch kv-replayer/feature/ssd-model-params
- load trace file: traces/prod/2024-09-12-hotkeys-anon.json (sanitized copy in S3 link in Confluence)
- run: ./replayer --burst-factor 8 --burst-duration 20 --ssd-cap 50 --mix heavy-long --seed 1421
- capture perf: ./scripts/capture-all.sh run_b4

Unresolved TODOs (short):
- correlate with eviction telemetry from dedicated clusters (need export job)
- instrument host NVMe queue depth per-cpu domain (harder than expected)
- produce p99 latency attribution breakdown by miss vs compute time
